Summary of Research Results: • Conceptual design report • Detailed mass and energy balances demonstrating high-purity hydrogen • Process and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs) with major equipment and control schemes • Recommended modular design concepts favoring mobility • Proved viability of self-powered design requirement Task 1: Conduct Study on Power Needs for MSU Subtask 1:1 The participant will provide the Contractor with the relevant information to conduct the study outlined in task 1.2. This includes dimensions and materials plus operating conditions such as pressure and temperature for each MSU. Subtask 1.2 The contractor will conduct a study of the parasitic power required for a three-stage MSU (needed for 6-9’s purity) contemplating heat economizing from thermal sources within the overall Biomass Super Gasifier (BMSG) system. The Contractor will provide the study to the Participant, the Participant will review the study and provide feedback to the Contractor. The study will quantify power requirements, economize thermal energy, and create a flow chart of control design for a three-stage MSU. Most hydrogen off-take applications call for high purity hydrogen (e.g. 99.9999%), which will require a series of three individual MSU with interstage blowers because the native separation per stage is expected to be 99.5% with is sufficient for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) purity, but not the full spectrum of commercial applications. The project kicked off with a series of meaningful discussions with GFE to elucidate the operating conditions for the hydrogen purification process. Initial discussions focused on temperature and pressure requirements for an individual MSU stage. The first design task assessed mass and energy balances for a high-temperature (500-600°T), high-pressure (60-120 psig) process requiring significant heat recovery and economizing. By re-evaluating material properties and performance requirements, the Contractor recommended a moderate-temperature (< 200°C), low pressure (< 15 psig) process requiring minimal thermal management. This represents significant savings in terms of footprint, power requirements, capital expenditures, and operating expenses for the overall process.
